summary: A German question-word question puts the question word first and the conjugated verb second, then the subject: Was trinkst du? Wo ist der Bahnhof? Wer ist das? – the same “verb in second place” as in a statement, while a yes/no question puts the verb first (Trinkst du Tee?). All question words begin with w- (die W-Fragen): was (what), wer (who), wo (where), wann (when), wie (how), warum (why), wie viel / wie viele (how much / how many), welcher (which) and wessen (whose). Two of them decline. wer has cases like the article der: wer (subject), wen (object), wem (dative: mit wem?), wessen (whose). welcher declines like dieser: welcher Tee, welche Tasche, welches Buch, welchen Tee (accusative). A noun that belongs to the question word moves with it into first place: Welchen Tee möchten Sie? Wie viele Kinder haben Sie? wie viel goes with uncountable nouns (wie viel Zucker), wie viele with plurals (wie viele Kinder). wessen sounds formal; everyday German asks Von wem ist das? The jobs of this step answer Was sind Sie von Beruf? – with no article after sein: Ich bin Ärztin. Er ist Koch. German marks the sex of the person in the job word: der Arzt / die Ärztin, der Koch / die Köchin (-in, often with umlaut).

blocks.title: Verb second, not first
blocks.text: Was trinkst du? (question word + verb) – Trinkst du Tee? (verb first: yes/no). Never *Was du trinkst? in a main question: that order belongs to indirect questions (Ich weiß nicht, was du trinkst).

blocks.title: wer = who, wo = where
blocks.text: wer asks about a person (who), wo about a place (where); woher and wohin ask where from and where to. Wer ist das? – Wo ist das?

blocks.title: Asking the name and the job
blocks.text: Wie heißt du? / Wie heißen Sie? (literally “How are you called?”) – not *Was heißt du? · Was bist du von Beruf? / Was sind Sie von Beruf? – Ich bin Ingenieurin.

askYourself: What do I want to know? A person → wer; a thing → was; a place → wo; a time → wann; the manner → wie; the reason → warum; an amount → wie viel / wie viele; a choice → welcher; the owner → wessen / von wem.
Is the person I ask about the subject (wer), the object (wen) or after a dative preposition (mit wem, bei wem)?
Does a noun belong to the question word (welchen Tee, wie viele Kinder)? Then both go together into first place.
Can I count it? wie viele + plural; otherwise wie viel + singular.
Is the conjugated verb in second place, right after the question word?
Am I asking about a job? Was … von Beruf? – and the answer has no article: Ich bin Lehrerin.
Is the person a woman? Then the job word ends in -in (Ärztin, Köchin).
steps: Choose the question word (and its case or ending).
Put it first, with its noun if it has one.
Then the subject and the rest; end with ?

traps: Verb second, not first: Wo ist der Bahnhof? (not *Wo der Bahnhof ist? in a direct question).
wer is who, wo is where.
Wie heißt du? – not *Was heißt du? (Was heißt …? asks what a word means).
wen and wem: Für wen …? (für + accusative) – Mit wem …? (mit + dative).
wie viel + uncountable, wie viele + plural: wie viel Milch, wie viele Äpfel.
welcher takes the endings of dieser: Welchen Tee? (masculine accusative) – Welches Buch? (neuter).
No article before a job after sein: Ich bin Ärztin. – but Sie ist eine gute Ärztin.
A woman’s job word ends in -in: Arzt → Ärztin, Koch → Köchin, Anwalt → Anwältin (umlaut!).

quiz.why: German asks “How are you called?”: Wie heißt du?

quiz.q: ___ ist das? – Das ist mein Bruder.

quiz.why: mit takes the dative: mit wem.
Children can be counted: wie viele + plural.
der Tee is masculine and the object: welchen (like diesen).
Question word first, verb second, no “do”.
No article, and the feminine job word -in (with umlaut).

quiz.q: Whose bag is this? – the everyday way
quiz.why: wessen is formal; speech uses von wem.

seeAlso.note: Arabic also puts the question word first: mā / mādhā (what), man (who), ayna (where), matā (when), kayfa (how), li-mādhā (why), kam (how many, + a singular noun), ayy (which).
Hebrew question words come first too: ma, mi, eifo, matai, eikh, lama, kama, eize / eizo; “whose” is shel mi – literally “of whom”, like German von wem.
Chinese leaves the question word where the answer would be: 你喝什么？ (you drink what?) – no inversion, no verb movement.
A yes/no question puts the verb first; a W-question puts it second.

notes.text: The question word comes first in Greek too (Τι πίνεις;), and ποιος / ποιον / ποιου decline like wer / wen / wessen. German adds a strict rule: the verb right after the question word, then the subject. τι – was, ποιος – wer, πού – wo, πότε – wann, πώς – wie, γιατί – warum, πόσο / πόσοι – wie viel / wie viele.
Что ты пьёшь? puts the question word first as German does, but Russian lets the subject come before the verb; German never does: Was trinkst du? кто / кого / кому decline like wer / wen / wem.
¿Qué bebes? – question word first, then the verb, as in German: Was trinkst du? quién / quiénes is wer (for one or many).
German has no do: What do you drink? = Was trinkst du? wer looks like “where” but means “who”; “where” is wo. whose = wessen, but everyday German prefers Von wem ist das?
Spoken French can leave the question word in place (Tu bois quoi ?); German always puts it first, with the verb second: Was trinkst du?
Hindi leaves the question word in the place of the answer, before the verb (tum kyā pīte ho?); German moves it to the front: Was trinkst du?
Persian keeps the question word where the answer would be (to či mixori?); German puts it first, with the verb second.
Marathi keeps the question word in place (tū kāy pitos?); German moves it to the front, with the verb right after it.
Arabic also puts the question word first (mādhā tashrabu?); German adds the subject after the verb: Was trinkst du?
ma ata shote? puts the question word first, then the subject; German puts the verb before the subject: Was trinkst du?
Turkish keeps the question word before the verb at the end (Ne içiyorsun?); German puts it first and the verb second: Was trinkst du?
Japanese keeps the question word in place and adds ka (nani o nomimasu ka?); German moves the question word to the front.
Korean keeps the question word in place (mwo masyeoyo?); German puts it first, with the verb second.
Mitä juot? – question word first and verb second, exactly the German order: Was trinkst du?
The question word comes right before the verb (Mit iszol?), as in German, where the verb follows it at once: Was trinkst du?
The question word usually follows the verb (unakunywa nini?); German puts it first: Was trinkst du?
Chinese keeps the question word where the answer would be (你喝什么?); German moves it to the front and the verb follows: Was trinkst du?
Vietnamese leaves the question word in place (anh uống gì?); German puts it first.
Inuktitut uses question words together with question endings on the verb (Qanuippit? How are you?); German puts the question word first and the plain verb right after it: Wie geht es dir?
